extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional screenwriters and storytellers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and standards for designing, writing, and revising screen stories—covering substance, structure, style, and the professional craft required to create films of archetypal power and commercial/artistic viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is about principles, not rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule says, 'You must do it this way.' A principle says, 'This works ...and has through all remembered time.' The difference is crucial. Your work needn't be modeled after a particular prototype; rather, it must be well made within the principles that shape our art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mindlessly follow checklists or recipes; instead learn the underlying principles of story so you can make original choices that still 'work.' Rules may be obeyed or broken; principles are what make breaking rules meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is about eternal, universal forms, not formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single prototype or foolproof story model for commercial success; excellent films show an astounding variety of designs, yet they embody a universal form of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the universal form beneath diverse films rather than memorizing formulas. Recognize that different genres and styles can all realize the same deep form in unique ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is about archetypes, not stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: An archetypal story unearths a universally human experience and wraps it inside a unique, culture‑specific expression; a stereotypical story confines itself to narrow, culture‑specific clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for stories that reveal universal human conflicts through fresh, specific detail (examples: LIKE WATER FOR CHOCOLATE). Avoid recycling familiar settings, characters, and actions that produce clichés and limit audience empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness, not shortcuts (economy takes time)
rubrics_metrics.description: From inspiration to last draft you may need as much time to write a screenplay as to write a novel. Screenwriters must cut and cut again to express the maximum in the fewest possible words; brevity takes time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rework relentlessly; don't assume a screenplay is 'quicker' just because pages look sparse. Invest time in editing for economy and precision—Polish seals a script's integrity and reduces interference in production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft is learnable; focus on realities, not mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no hidden conspiracies or unsolvable secrets to writing—storycraft has explicit principles (Aristotle onward). The camera magnifies falsity; a screenplay can't hide holes behind language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study established principles and practice them scene by scene. Expect difficulty but not mystery: technical mastery and determination allow the puzzle to yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the art, not second‑guess the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot reliably predict what will sell; success comes from writing with surpassing quality rather than chasing trends or imitation of recent hits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate on achieving excellence and originality. Agents and producers seek distinctive, well-made work; polished, mature scripts are optioned and produced more often than quick knockoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the audience; keep ahead of their perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences are intelligent and sensitive; they anticipate and perceive more than many writers think. You must shape your story to express your vision while satisfying audience desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid underestimating viewers. Structure beats, revelations, and dramatic strategy should stay ahead of audience expectations—surprise without insulting intelligence; use craft to manage audience anticipation and reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality = confluence of content and form; avoid eccentricity for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality arises from distinctive subject matter (content) combined with a unique selection and arrangement of events (form). Difference alone is not originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop both fresh subject matter and an idiosyncratic shaping of events. Do not use gimmicks or 'art movie' quirkiness merely to call attention to yourself; style must be inseparable from vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design story around protagonist, desire, antagonism, progression, and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The core design questions: Who are these characters? What do they want? Why do they want it? How do they try to get it? What stops them? What are the consequences? Designing story—spine, progression, crisis, climax, resolution—is the overwhelming creative task (75%+ of effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarifying protagonist and desire, structuring antagonism, arranging turning points and climaxes, and ensuring logical progression so each scene advances the spine of the story toward meaningful consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common story problems (weak motivation, exposition, holes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical failures include heavy expository openings, convenient coincidence, weak or absent protagonist, unrelated tensions that never develop, characters who are never revealed to be more than they seem, lack of insight, and predictable or lifeless episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose and eliminate false motivation, redundant characters, empty subtext, and plot holes. Ensure tight motivation, connected subplots, and scenes that reveal character and meaning rather than merely describe or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn through study, apprenticeship, and reflection—not just 'instinct' or imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many novices mistake absorbed habits from prior reading/watching for instinct; real craft comes from study (books, theatre, film analysis), apprenticeship, and disciplined practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue deliberate study of dramaturgy and technique, seek mentorship or rigorous editorial feedback, and combine life experience with deep self‑reflection to inform your storytelling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form is changeless but not a formula—grasp universal form
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an innate universal form of story that is changeless across cultures and ages; understanding this form is essential, but it must not be reduced to a mechanical recipe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internalize the universal components of story so you can invent varied, original structures; resist treating form as a formula that guarantees results—use it as a guiding architecture for creative choices.
